title: Keeping Time
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of timekeeping from early shadow-based methods through sundials, water clocks, incense and candle clocks, astrolabes, hourglasses, mechanical clocks with the verge and foliot escapement, pendulum clocks, anchor escapements, grandfather clocks, and wristwatches, ending with a note on quartz and atomic clocks. The episode also includes a tour announcement, a correction about a listener's anniversary count, and a listener mail question from Bill about whether the Akron live show is appropriate for his eleven-year-old son.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live tour

segments.title: Tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming tour stops in Denver, Seattle and San Francisco and direct listeners to the website for tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Welcome and introduction to the episode on timekeeping, which Olivia helped research.

segments.title: Shadows, gnomons and early timekeeping
segments.summary: Early humans tracked time with shadows cast by a stick (gnomon). Timekeeping began as seasonal and astrological tracking rather than appointment keeping. The Chinese northern archaeological find dates to about 2300 BC, and the Egyptian shadow clock (T-shaped) is discussed.

segments.title: Sundials and the hemicycle
segments.summary: Anaximander's sundial in sixth century BC, Greek hour-marking sundials around 350 BCE, and the hemicycle sundial around 280 BCE, which accounted for seasonal sun changes with multiple arcs. Greek seasonal (unequal) hours are explained.

segments.title: Seasonal hours and portable sundials
segments.summary: Greek seasonal hours lasted into the medieval period, lengthening in summer and shortening in winter. Portable bronze sundials with latitude settings were made, and some Muslim sundials were developed for prayer times.

segments.title: Islamic sundials and uniform hours
segments.summary: Muslims adopted sundials for prayer times and developed trigonometry-based designs including conical sundials. Abu al-Hasan al-Marrakushi in the early thirteenth century promoted uniform hours.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break between segments.

segments.title: Water clocks
segments.summary: Water clocks were used across cultures, with problems from freezing and viscosity changes. Engineers added floats, valves and siphons. A Chinese engineer in the tenth century used mercury instead of water.

segments.title: Incense clocks
segments.summary: Incense clocks, dating to at least the sixth century CE in China, used burning incense as a timer, with maze-like boxes and scent markers for different hours. Incense was also used as a fuse-based alarm.

segments.title: Candle clocks, astrolabes and hourglasses
segments.summary: Alfred the Great reportedly timed his day with six candles. Astrolabes, invented by Muslims around the sixth century CE, could be used to keep time. Hourglasses appeared much later, with the earliest known reference in Italy in 1338.

segments.title: Ancient inventors and water clock showpieces
segments.summary: Andronikos of Kyrrhos built the Tower of Winds in Athens, combining water clocks, sundials and wind gauges. Inventors added showy features to timekeeping devices.

segments.title: Chinese astronomical clock tower and al-Jazari's elephant clock
segments.summary: An eighth century CE Chinese Buddhist monk built a water-powered gear clock with bells; Su Song's eleventh century clock tower had mannequins ringing gongs; al-Jazari's elephant clock and castle clock are described.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: Early mechanical clocks and weight-driven escapements
segments.summary: Chinese water clocks may have been the first mechanical clocks. Gerbert of Aurillac (later Pope Sylvester II) is said to have built a mechanical device in 996, though this is doubted. European clocks replaced water with falling weights.

segments.title: Verge and foliot mechanism
segments.summary: The verge and foliot mechanism regulated falling weights so gears turned at a steady rate, creating a ticking sound. Comparison to the drum in the movie The Karate Kid Part II is made.

segments.title: Monasteries, church clocks and bells
segments.summary: Early European clocks helped monks keep time for daily prayers. Church steeples were tall to house clock weights. The Salisbury Cathedral clock from 1386 is the oldest surviving mechanical clock and had no face.

segments.title: Clocks and modern life
segments.summary: Once clocks had faces, people read time directly. Lewis Mumford's view that clocks marked the birth of the modern era is discussed. The minute as a unit came into use in the late fourteenth century.

segments.title: Springs and early inaccuracy
segments.summary: Coiled springs replaced weights, making clocks portable, but friction and humidity made them inexact. Galileo used his pulse to measure pendulum swings.

segments.title: Pendulum clocks and anchor escapement
segments.summary: Galileo's pendulum insight; Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656. Robert Hooke introduced the anchor escapement, reducing the swing arc. William Clement added a minute hand in 1680, producing the long case clock.

segments.title: Grandfather clocks and quartz
segments.summary: The long case clock got the name grandfather clock from the 1876 song My Grandfather's Clock by Henry Clay Work. Quartz crystal oscillation later led to watches and atomic clocks, which underpin GPS and phone time.

segments.title: Henry Clay People aside
segments.summary: Hosts mention the band Henry Clay People, friends of the show, who wrote the show's TV theme.

segments.title: Wristwatches, stopwatches and luminescence
segments.summary: Pocket watches came first; wristwatches became common after the late nineteenth century and especially after World War One. Stopwatch functions, the Rolex Oyster waterproof watch of 1926, and luminous watches are discussed. Chronographs and the horoscope etymology are mentioned.
